newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Shadowy Republican group says responsible for bombs.
newsitem.headline: Shadowy Republican group says responsible for bombs.

text.p: A shadowy Irish Republican group claimed credit on Tuesday for the bombing of Britain's Northern Ireland army headquarters but failed to give a recognised codeword.

A spokesman for Ireland's semi-state RTE broadcasting network said a caller purporting to speak for the Continuity Army Council (CAC) rang shortly before the midday news bulletin to claim repsonsibility for Monday's Lisburn barracks blast.
But the caller failed to give a codeword which guerrilla groups, media organisations and broadcasting networks use to identify bona-fide bomb claims and bomb warnings
RTE said the caller also claimed that 27-year-old Irishman Diarmuid O'Neill, killed by British police in a London raid last month, was one of its activists.
O'Neill was killed when police uncovered a huge suspected IRA arms haul which police said was being primed for an imminent attack on British targets.
Analysts were sceptical of the caller's claims, arguing that only a recognised password would have authenticated them.
"This could have been anyone in a Dublin or Belfast pub," commented Ed Moloney, Northern Ireland editor of Dublin's Sunday Tribune newspaper.
The CAC came to light last year when police intercepted a huge car bomb being driven across the border towards a British army barracks at Crossmaglen.

In July this year the same organisation claimed responsibility for a massive car bomb outside a hotel at Killyhevlin, Northern Ireland, during high tension between Catholics and Protestants over Orange Order marches.
Irish security sources believe the CAC has links to the Irish Republican Socialist Party, a hardline left-wing organisation which broke away from mainstream Sinn Fein in the 1970s.

The British government, Northern Irish police and security forces say the Irish Republican Army (IRA), Sinn Fein's military ally, is the prime suspect in the Lisburn bombing, and are suspicious of rival claims.
Last week Belfast police blew up a large car bomb planted in a Belfast street and said the CAC claimed credit for leaving it there.

Security experts say whoever bombed the Lisburn barracks must have had intimate knowledge of its layout, gained over a long period, as well as the expertise to plant two devices timed to go off sequentially to cause maximum injuries.
"This Continuity crowd is still at the alarm clock (detonator) stage, I think," Moloney, an acknowledged expert on the Northern Ireland security scene, commented.

The IRA is thought to have several hundred activists trained to carry out security attacks, large arms caches mainly in the Irish Republic, and a network of safe houses stretching from the island of Ireland through Britain and Western Europe.
Despite several recent police successes in uncovering stockpiles of detonators and its favoured Semtex plastic explosive, police say the IRA has enough weaponry to fight into the 21st century.
